newsitem.title: USA: NYSEG transition plan includes discounts.
newsitem.headline: NYSEG transition plan includes discounts.

text.p: New York State Electric & Gas Corp said on Friday that its transition to competition proposal calls for a five year rate freeze while allowing most customers to increase electricity use at half the present price.
The proposal, which seeks to move toward competition at a slower rate than proposed by state regulators, calls for functional separation of generation from other operations.
The utility said the rate freeze, proposed to start August 1, 1997, depends on NYSEG being allowed to raise prices 2.8 percent this year and 2.7 percent in 1997.
In late August, the New York Public Service Commission postponed a decision on a rate structure proposed by NYSEG to implement this year's 2.8 percent increase.

This action was cited by several utility sources as one of the reasons the Energy Association of New York filed suit last week challenging the industry restructuring proposal resulting from the commission's Competitive Opportunities Proceeding.

As part of that proceeding, the commission put forward its proposals in May, requesting proposals from individual utilities by October 1. NYSEG was the first to respond, filing its proposal, which it calls NYSEPlan, Friday.

"We strongly support competition and NYSEGPlan is designed to treat customers and shareholders fairly during the transition to competition," said executive vice president Jack H. Roskoz. "It would provide customers with stable prices and safe, reliable service. Shareholders would continue to have a reasonable opportunity to fully recover prudent investments."
Retail competition would be phased in under NYSEGPlan, beginning August 1, 1998, the utility said.

"After one year of retail competition in areas yet to be selected, we would work with customers and other parties...to assess its success. The schedule for expanding retail competition to all customers in the NYSEG service area would be reviewed during that collaborative effort," Roskoz said.
NYSEGPlan calls for wholesale competition to begin August 1, 1997, the utility said. That's eight months later than the commission proposed.

"In today's energy marketplace most electric utilities own generating stations and use the power from those stations to serve their customers. Under wholesale competition, we would functionally separate our generating stations from the rest of our operations. The plants would then compete in an unregulated market," Roskoz said.
